young.html: James George Frazer was a Scottish scholar who spent his whole life in libraries, reading travelers' reports, old histories and letters from missionaries all over the world. He collected thousands of customs and stories, and asked why people in faraway places did such similar things.

Here is one pattern he noticed. In many places, people tried to make things happen by copying them: sprinkling water to bring rain, or jumping high so the crops would grow tall. Frazer called that the idea that "like produces like." In other places, people believed that things that once touched stay connected, so they kept a lost tooth or a lock of hair safe. He called these two ideas the laws of magic.

young.html: Lucky habits. Many people today have small lucky habits: a lucky sock, crossing fingers, not stepping on cracks. Ask your family what lucky habits they know. Which ones are about copying, and which are about touching? (Frazer would have been very interested!)

full.html: James George Frazer (1854–1941) was a classical scholar at Trinity College, Cambridge. The Golden Bough began as two volumes in 1890, grew to twelve by 1915, and was cut down by Frazer himself to the one-volume abridged edition of 1922, the form most people read. It compares myths, rites and customs from ancient Greece and Rome, Europe's countryside and peoples all over the world.

full.text: Who does not know Turner's picture of the Golden Bough? The scene, suffused with the golden glow of imagination in which the divine mind of Turner steeped and transfigured even the fairest natural landscape, is a dream-like vision of the little woodland lake of Nemi—"Diana's Mirror," as it was called by the ancients.

full.html: Near this lake south of Rome stood a sacred grove of the goddess Diana. Ancient writers said its priest, called the King of the Wood, held his office until a challenger broke a branch from a certain tree and overcame him. Frazer sets out to explain this strange rule, and the explanation becomes a tour of the world's customs.

full.text: If we analyse the principles of thought on which magic is based, they will probably be found to resolve themselves into two: first, that like produces like, or that an effect resembles its cause; and, second, that things which have once been in contact with each other continue to act on each other at a distance after the physical contact has been severed.
full.author: James George Frazer
full.work: The Golden Bough (abridged edition), Chapter III
full.note: text of the one-volume abridged edition of 1922, from a later printing

full.html: Frazer calls the first the Law of Similarity (behind "homoeopathic" or imitative magic) and the second the Law of Contact or Contagion (behind contagious magic). Together he calls them sympathetic magic.

full.html: Frazer saw a grand pattern. Magic, he argued, is a mistaken kind of science: it assumes nature follows fixed rules people can control, but has the rules wrong. When people find magic fails, they turn to religion, seeking the favor of higher powers. Later, science returns to the idea of a fixed order of nature, now with rules tested by observation.

full.text: The movement of the higher thought, so far as we can trace it, has on the whole been from magic through religion to science.

full.html: Along the way Frazer gathers stories of sacred kings, harvest customs, festivals of fire and the ancient myths of gods of vegetation who die and return with the seasons. The golden bough itself, he concludes, was the mistletoe.

The Golden Bough was hugely popular and shaped how educated readers thought about myth for decades. Poets and novelists borrowed from it: T. S. Eliot named it in the notes to The Waste Land. Anthropologists, though, came to reject much of it. Frazer never did fieldwork; he compared customs torn from their settings, often from unreliable reports, and his students, above all Bronisław Malinowski, insisted on living for years among the people one studies. The neat sequence from magic to religion to science is no longer accepted: all three exist side by side in many societies, and rites are not simply failed science. Wittgenstein objected that Frazer made other peoples' rituals look like stupid mistakes when they express something more. Scholars of religion have also questioned his grouping of different gods as one "dying and rising" type. Frazer hinted that Christian beliefs could be placed among his comparisons, which offended many readers then; later scholars questioned the comparisons themselves on historical grounds. The book remains a landmark in the history of anthropology, read now as much for what it shows about its own age as about the customs it describes.
Thinking Frazer visited the peoples he wrote about. He worked from books and letters in Cambridge, which is one reason later anthropologists distrusted his conclusions.

items: Virgil's Aeneid, on the Rome rungs, gave Frazer his title: Aeneas must pluck a golden bough before he can visit the underworld.
Herodotus also compared the customs of many peoples, and noticed how each thinks its own the best.
Lévi-Strauss, a later rung, studied myths as structures with their own logic, a very different method from Frazer's.
Eliot's Waste Land, in the literature rungs, drew on Frazer's vegetation myths.

questions: What lucky or traditional habits does your family have? Where did they come from?
Why might people in places far apart come up with similar customs?
Frazer studied other peoples only from books. What might he have missed?
Is it fair to call another culture's rituals "mistakes"? Why did Wittgenstein object?
Virgil's hero needed a golden bough to enter the underworld. What other stories have a magic object that opens a door?
care: The book describes many rites, including some violent ones; this rung keeps to its main ideas and gentle examples.
